extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and educated readers interested in aesthetic and moral criteria for literature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles for judging/producing literary work (essays, poetry, fiction) as articulated in Chesterton's criticism of 'progress', Kipling, and Shaw — emphasizing moral definition, poetic attention to common things, rootedness, discipline, consistency, and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress requires a defined moral doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: “Progress…is unmeaning without the previous definition of a moral doctrine, and … can only be applied to groups of persons who hold that doctrine in common.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton argues that the term 'progress' is illegitimate unless one knows the direction it implies — i.e., unless one has a definite creed and cast-iron code of morals. Anti-pattern: using 'progress' as a vague comparative opposed to precise moral ideals. Scoring note: claims about 'progress' should be grounded in an explicit moral or doctrinal framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress implies doctrinal certainty (direction matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Progress by its very name indicates a direction; and the moment we are in the least doubtful about the direction, we become in the same degree doubtful about the progress.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of progress by whether they commit to a clear direction; doubt about direction undermines the legitimacy of calling something progress. Example pitfalls: advocating 'more of nobody knows what.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of wonder: make even common subjects poetic
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award literary work that treats ordinary objects/events with sustained enthusiasm and discovery (the 'bore' who finds blades of grass splendid). Anti-patterns: literary refinement that has made common things prosaic; lack of curiosity or interest in the quotidian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, evocative names and images
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton contrasts meaningful names (e.g., 'Smith' — 'made of iron and flame') with empty, fanciful names (e.g., 'Aylmer Valence'), arguing that names can carry history, industry, and poetic force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer character/place names and tangible imagery that evoke social history and embodied life. Example guidance: a 'Smith' conveys hammer, trade, epic resonance; avoid meaningless, decorative names that fail to ground a character in reality or symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recover poetry in industrial/low elements (steam, slang)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kipling 'pierced through to the romantic, imaginative matter of the things themselves' and 'perceived the significance and philosophy of steam and of slang.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise works that find the 'divine parentage' in apparently base or modern things (machinery, slang, trades). Anti-pattern: dismissing industrial or colloquial elements as merely materialistic or unpoetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author should have a definite view or message
rubrics_metrics.description: “Above all, he has had something to say, a definite view of things to utter, and that always means that a man is fearless and faces everything.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writers who take a coherent stance or possess a discernible thesis — even if they err. Anti-pattern: empty eclecticism or changeable opinions presented as depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict discipline and interdependence (romance of division of labour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kipling’s chief theme is 'the romance of the division of labour and the discipline of all the trades' — praising the baker, tailor, engineers as much as soldiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works for their attention to organized, communal effort and the dignity of ordinary trades. Reward accurate, sympathetic portrayal of everyday workmanship and discipline; avoid valorizing only martial courage while ignoring peaceful crafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rootedness and local belonging confer depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton: 'The man in the cabbage field has seen nothing at all; but he is thinking of the things that unite men… The man in his own kitchen-garden, with fairyland opening at the gate, is the man with large ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value literature grounded in place and commitment; rooted attachment (patriotism/locale) produces tragic finality and depth. Anti-pattern: cosmopolitan touristiness that treats cultures superficially and 'makes the world small.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep understanding requires patience and humility, not tourist haste
rubrics_metrics.description: “If we wish to understand [other civilizations] it must not be as tourists or inquirers, it must be with the loyalty of children and the great patience of poets.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer approaches that study cultures/people closely (microscopic attention) rather than glib, panoramic travel-writing. Penalize superficial, conquering, or instrumental representations of other peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness even when eccentric
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton notes that Shaw's insistence on telling strict truth makes him appear eccentric: 'That too truthful man… is Mr. Bernard Shaw.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit writers who report or depict uncomfortable truths faithfully, even if it seems odd to contemporaneous sensibilities. Caveat: truthfulness should be balanced with humility (see other metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual consistency and even application of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Shaw's strength: 'his power consists in holding his own fortress night and day… his scales, such as they are, are held even, and that his law, such as it is, is justly enforced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value thinkers and writers who apply their principles uniformly (criticize lawlessness in all camps, not selectively). Award coherence of standards and predictability of intellectual stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization and moral ideals are legitimate and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton counters Shaw's old doctrine by asserting that forbidding strict moral ideals is itself an iron rule; 'Making generalizations is what makes him a man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of general moral rules and ideals in human thought and literature; anti-pattern: reflexive hostility to generalization presented as intellectual liberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for humble, delighted appreciation of ordinary humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief defect in Shaw is 'he is not easily pleased' — Chesterton urges that 'genuine appreciation rests on a certain mystery of humility' and that 'little things please great minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward works/authors who exhibit humility, delight, and capacity to be pleased by small, mundane wonders. Penalize perpetual superiority, priggish comparison to an imagined 'superman', or constant dismissal of humanity for failing to meet an impossible ideal.
